p: Tablet II is pieced together from many copies; this stretch begins on a Neo-Assyrian fragment.
b: No single copy of Tablet II survives whole. SEAL arranges the pieces in story order as segments A to I. This chapter is segment E. It begins on the back of Q, a small Neo-Assyrian fragment (Sm. 292), and SEAL says no one knows how many lines are missing before it. From 7:9 on, the Late Babylonian copy from Sippar (be) and the Old Babylonian copies B and D take over. SEAL numbers the lines after the Old Babylonian copies and be, so a few lines found in only one copy carry letters (7:44 is line E 43a).

p: The copies of this chapter call the god Ea; the Plain keeps 'Enki' all through the book.
b: Enki is the god's Sumerian name, Ea his Akkadian one, and the copies use both. The Old Babylonian copies of Atrahasis mostly write Enki; the later ones, and here even the Old Babylonian B and D in places, write Ea. The site keeps one name, Enki, so the reader is not misled into thinking there are two gods. Where a copy has Ea, as in 7:9, 7:75, 7:79 and most of chapter 8 in the late copies, the Akkadian is given in the notes and variants.
orig: {d}é-a (Ea)

p: Atrahasis is the god's servant, the same word the Bible uses for those who serve the LORD.
b: The word is ardu, 'slave' or 'servant'. Atrahasis belongs to Enki the way a worker belongs to his master, and Enki speaks to him alone. The Bible gives the title 'my servant' to people who stand close to God: Abraham, Moses, Job, David. But the relation is different. Enki uses his servant to outwit the other gods. The LORD calls his servants to share his own plans: "unless he has shown his secret counsel / to his servants the prophets" (Amos 3:7).
orig: ardi(ÌR)-šu (ardišu), 'his servant'

a: The ruling is heard; the assembly sits.
p: The gods meet as a court and give a ruling. Christians read such councils in more than one way.
b: Dīnu is a court case or verdict, and puḫru is the gods' assembly. In Babylon the high gods ran the world like a council of elders. The Bible also pictures God surrounded by a heavenly court: "among the gods he passes judgment" (Psalm 82:1). Christian readers take that picture in different ways: some see only angels; some, the "divine council" readers, see in the gods of the nations real spiritual powers set under God and judged by him (Psalm 82:6–7). In Atrahasis there is no one above the council. Its rulings are made by vote and can be dodged.
orig: di-nu šá-kín pu-uḫ-ru (dīnu šakin puḫru), 'the case, the assembly is set'

p: The gods bind themselves by oath; the oath will matter again before the Flood.
b: The Akkadian says the gods 'brought their mouth' to an oath, an idiom for agreeing. SEAL notes that the order of words is unusual. An oath of the gods runs through Tablet II: Enlil reminds the gods that they all swore together (9:15, 9:29) and finally makes them swear to the flood (9:78), and Enki refuses to be bound (9:140). Once sworn, a god's oath could not simply be taken back, so Enki looks for ways around it.
orig: ub-lam pi-i-šu-nu i-lu ma-a-mi-tam, 'they brought their mouth, the gods, an oath'

a: The elders at the set time
p: The late copy here misread an older line about gathering the elders in Atrahasis' house.
b: Only be, the Late Babylonian copy, keeps 7:13–14, and SEAL argues that its scribe misunderstood his model. The Old Babylonian form of this speech, in Tablet I (5:36–37), has Enki tell Atrahasis to call the elders together 'in your house'. The late scribe divided the signs wrongly, read 'in the middle of the counsel' and wrote 'gathered' for 'gather'. The Plain translates be as it stands; the sense is the same order Enki gave the first time.
orig: qer-bi-tum mil-ki (qerbītum milki), 'the middle of the counsel'

p: The heralds are to make noise, the same word as the human noise that keeps Enlil awake.
b: Rigmu is the 'noise' or 'cry' of humankind that troubles Enlil (7:67, 7:70). Here Enki's plan answers noise with noise: the heralds are to 'make noise appear' in the land. The poem plays on the word. The noise that annoys Enlil is the sound of a crowded, living world; the noise of the heralds is a public call to change whom the people serve. The site renders rigmu as 'noise' every time so the play can be seen.
orig: ri-ig-ma (rigma), 'noise'

t: Worship one god, as a tactic
p: Enki tells the people to drop every god but the one who can end the drought. The Bible's 'one God' is different.
b: Enki's advice sounds like the first commandment, but it is a tactic. The people are to stop honoring their own gods and goddess and bring all their gifts to Adad, the god who holds back the rain, so that the gift will shame him into acting (7:38). Nothing is said about which god is true. Elijah also told Israel to choose one: "If the LORD is the God, go after him. If Baal is, go after him" (1 Kings 18:21). There the choice is about who is real. Here it is about who can be bought.

p: Adad was the Babylonian god of storm and rain. His name lives on in the Bible as Hadad.
b: Adad (written with the sign IŠKUR) was the god of storms, thunder and rain. In a land that lived by rivers and canals, rain still decided the harvest in the north and the pasture everywhere. His name, Hadad in the West, appears in the Bible inside Aramean royal names such as "Ben-hadad" (1 Kings 15:18) and in the place or rite of "Hadad-rimmon" (Zechariah 12:11). To 'look for his door' is to go to his temple with gifts.
orig: {d}adad(IŠKUR)-ma (Adad)

p: Babylonians fed their gods with bread, flour and drink. The Bible's God needs no food.
b: Epītu is a baked loaf, and the next line adds maṣḫatu, a flour used in offerings. In Mesopotamia the gods' statues were served meals every day in their temples, and Atrahasis shows why that mattered: when humans suffer, the gods' tables are empty. The Bible keeps offerings of bread and flour (Leviticus 2), but it denies that God eats them: "Do I feed on the flesh of strong bulls? / Do I drink goats' blood?" (Psalm 50:13).
orig: ye-pí-tam (epītam), 'a baked loaf'

p: Dew falls unseen at night, so the god who sends it comes like a thief.
b: SEAL explains the picture: dew settles in the dark, unnoticed, the way a thief slips in, and so the field 'like a thief' will quietly bring a big crop (7:24). In a dry land dew mattered. The Bible counts it among God's gifts, "some of the dew of the sky" (Genesis 27:28), and its loss among his warnings: "these coming years will have no dew and no rain unless I give the word" (1 Kings 17:1).
orig: li-iš-ta?-ri-iq-ma (lištarriqma), 'let him steal in'

p: In the poem rain is pried from a god with gifts. In the Bible God gives it freely, even to the ungrateful.
b: Atrahasis' town gets its rain by flattering the right god. The Bible names one Giver: "Can any of the nations' empty idols make it rain?" (Jeremiah 14:22). Paul told the people of Lystra that God "did not leave himself without a witness," "giving you rains from the sky and seasons that bear fruit" (Acts 14:17), and Jesus said the Father "sends rain on righteous and unrighteous people" (Matthew 5:45). Rain is not a bribe returned but a kindness meant to lead people to the Giver.

p: The late copy says Atrahasis gathered the elders at his house; Tablet I says at his gate.
b: In the parallel line of Tablet I (5:49) the Old Babylonian copy has Atrahasis gather the elders 'at his gate' (ana bābišu), the place where elders met. Here be writes 'to his house'. The meaning is close: a leader calls the town's elders to his home to give them a message. The Bible's elders also met 'at the gate' (Ruth 4:1–2).
orig: ab-bi-tiš?-šu (ana bītišu), 'to his house'

t: A gift that shames a god
p: The gift is meant to shame Adad into doing good in return. The Bible's God takes no bribe.
b: The verb is bâšu, 'to be ashamed'. The people overwhelm Adad with gifts until he feels obliged to repay them, the way a gift binds a person in the ancient world. Proverbs knows the method among humans: "a bribe tucked in the robe, even fierce rage" (Proverbs 21:14). Moses says it cannot work on God: "He does not play favorites, and he does not take a bribe" (Deuteronomy 10:17). Offerings in the Bible are thanks and worship, not leverage (Micah 6:6–8).
orig: li-⌈ba-aš⌉-m[a (libāšma), 'let him be ashamed'

t: Passing a hand over the gift
p: The gesture is not certain: probably Adad accepts the gift by touching it.
b: The verb šukkulu is rare here. SEAL understands the line as the god passing his hand over the gift, a sign that he accepts it. Other scholars have taken the verb as 'to wipe' or tied it to another root (SEAL's notes on the parallel lines of Tablet II, segment A). The point is clear either way: the god takes the gift, and the rain follows.
orig: li-ša-⌈ak⌉-[ki-il] qá-a[s-sú] (lišakkil qāssu), 'let him pass his hand'

t: A temple built for one god
p: The elders build Adad a temple in the city. SEAL notes that no such temple is known in the real town.
b: 'House' (bītu) is the usual word for a temple: the god's home, with a door (7:19) and a table. SEAL notes that the line names no city, but the story implies Shuruppak, Atrahasis' town in the later flood stories, and that no temple of Adad is known there from the lists of temples. Solomon, dedicating the LORD's house, said what no Babylonian builder said: "the heavens, the heavens above the heavens, are not big enough for you. Then how could this house I built be enough!" (1 Kings 8:27).
orig: ib-nu-ú bi-[is-su] (ibnû bīssu), 'they built his house'

p: The start of this line is broken; the word 'not' comes from the parallel lines.
b: Only the end of the verb and part of 'their goddess' survive here. The negative stood in the break. It is supplied from the matching lines of Enki's order and Atrahasis' speech (7:18, 7:34) and from the same line in Tablet I (5:70), where the story is told the same way. Without it the line would say the opposite of what the people did.
orig: ú]-⌈se⌉-[el-lu-ú (usellû), 'they pleaded'

p: The bribed god pays back with a huge crop. The Bible tells of large harvests as God's blessing.
b: 'Ninefold' (or 'twins' in the late copy) means a harvest far above normal. The Bible tells of Isaac in a famine year: "he reaped a hundred times what he sowed. The LORD blessed him" (Genesis 26:12), and Jesus speaks of seed that gave "a hundred times as much" (Matthew 13:8). The difference is the source: blessing given by a faithful God, not a return on a gift.

p: The verb may mean the people's looks 'came back' or 'grew bright'.
b: The copies write ittūru, which looks like 'they returned'. SEAL argues that it goes back to ittawrū, 'they became bright', the usual idiom with zīmū, 'looks' or 'face', and that one copy of the same line in Tablet I (5:81) has the form ittamrū from that verb. So the line may mean 'their faces shone again' after the hunger.
orig: zi-mu]-ši-na it-tu-ru (zīmūšina ittūrū), 'their looks returned (or: shone)'

p: Births return. In the Bible it is the LORD who opens the womb.
b: Rēmu means both 'womb' and 'compassion' (see 8:101). The drought had closed wombs too (6:30, 6:42); now births come again, and so does the noise. In Genesis the opening of the womb is God's personal gift: "he opened her womb" (Genesis 29:31). The difference grows sharp at the end of the poem, when the gods limit births to keep humans few (chapter 12), while in Genesis God blesses after the Flood: "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth" (Genesis 9:1).
orig: re-e-mu pe-ti (rēmu peti), 'the womb was open'

p: The late copy says 'three shars', 10,800 years. Other copies give other numbers.
b: A šār is 3,600, the big unit of Babylonian counting by sixties, so three are 10,800 years. In Tablet I the gap between troubles is '600 + 600' years (5:82), and at the start of Tablet II the Old Babylonian copy has 1,200 again while the Assyrian copy Q has 3,600 (6:1). The copies did not agree on the number. Alan Millard mentions a suggestion that Genesis' 120 years, "Their days will be 120 years" (Genesis 6:3), also belongs to a count by sixties, and compares the gaps between the troubles in Atrahasis.
orig: še-lal-ti šá-a-ri šá-na (šelalti šāri šanāti), 'three shars of years'

p: In Genesis growing many is a blessing. Here it brings back the noise that the gods hate.
b: The words match the first lines of Tablet II (6:2) and Tablet I (5:2). Genesis tells the same fact, "When humankind began to grow many" (Genesis 6:1), but it never treats numbers as the problem. God commands it: "Be fruitful, grow many, fill the earth" (Genesis 9:1). What God judges in Genesis is evil and violence (Genesis 6:5, 11). In Atrahasis the people are guilty of nothing worse than being alive and many.

a: At their noise the gods grew gloomy.
p: The old line spoke of 'the god', Enlil. The late scribes read the word as plural.
b: SEAL notes that the verb here is singular while the late copy writes 'gods' with a plural sign. In the Old Babylonian form of the line (6:4) ilu meant 'the god', that is Enlil, whose sleep is disturbed. The Neo-Assyrian scribe of Q also read it as plural and misunderstood the verb. The Plain translates the late copy as it stands.
orig: ilu(DINGIR{meš}) it-ta-aʾ-dar (ilū ittaʾdar), 'the gods grew gloomy'

p: Was humanity's noise a sin, or just the sound of too many people? Readers differ.
b: The poem never calls the noise a sin; it is the sound of crowded life that keeps Enlil awake. Some readers have taken it as rebellion or wrongdoing, to bring it closer to Genesis. Alan Millard thought it unlikely that the poem's 'din' equals the violence of Genesis 6, but held that 'the idea of disturbing deity' is common to both stories as the cause of the Flood. A Christian reading notes the gap: Genesis names the cause plainly, "the earth was full of violence" (Genesis 6:11).

p: The verb form shows Enlil calling the assembly over and over.
b: Ištanakkan is an iterative form: an action repeated. Enlil keeps calling the gods together. It is a small, telling picture of a ruler who cannot rest and cannot solve his problem, and has to win the others to each new plan. The old copies at 6:5 say instead that Enlil 'heard their uproar'.
orig: iš-ta-na-ka-an pu-ḫur-šu (ištanakkan puḫuršu), 'he kept setting his assembly'

t: Gods of the nations: nothing or demons?
p: Enlil's 'sons' are the gods of Babylon. Christians have read such gods in three ways.
b: The Bible speaks of the gods of the nations in three ways, and Christian readers weigh them together. They are nothing, made by hands: "Their idols are silver and gold" (Psalm 115:4). Yet worship given to them goes to evil spirits: "they sacrifice to demons and not to God" (1 Corinthians 10:20; Deuteronomy 32:17). And some read Psalm 82, where God judges "sons of the Most High," as a council of spiritual powers that went wrong. Justin Martyr held that demons had once made people worship them as gods (First Apology 5). These are readings, not the poem's meaning.

t: Locking the sky and the deep
p: Enlil locks the world from top to bottom. Genesis tells of the sky and the deep being opened and shut.
b: Enlil posts guards on each level of the world so that no help can reach humans: rain from the sky, water from below, fish from the sea. Genesis uses the same picture of a world with water above and below, but for the Flood itself: "all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the windows of the sky were opened" (Genesis 7:11), and at the end "The springs of the deep and the windows of the sky were shut, and the rain from the sky was held back" (Genesis 8:2). In Genesis one God holds every key.

t: The moon god and the underworld god
p: Late copies give the earth to Sin and Nergal. In the old copies Enlil guards it himself.
b: Sin was the moon god and Nergal the god of the underworld. SEAL notes that in the Old Babylonian copies Enlil says 'I guarded the lower earth' (9:17), and that later scribes gave his part to Sin and Nergal and changed 'lower' earth into 'middle' earth, a sign that their picture of the world had changed (Lambert; Horowitz). One Middle Babylonian copy still names Enlil (variant at 7:77). The Bible makes the moon a lamp, made on the fourth day (Genesis 1:16), and forbids its worship (Deuteronomy 4:19).
orig: {d}sîn(30) u {d}nergal(U.GUR) (Sin u Nergal), 'Sin and Nergal'

a: The bolt, the barrier of the sea,
p: Enki holds the bar that keeps the sea in. Job and the Psalms give that bar to God.
b: The 'bolt' (šigaru) and 'barrier' or 'trap' (naḫbalu) of the sea were Enki's charge from the start, when the gods drew lots (1:15). Alan Millard notes that the sea here is the common noun, not the dragon Tiamat, and that there is no battle, only an unruly element that must be held in. He compares the Bible's passages on God confining the sea. God asks Job, "Who closed doors to hold back the sea," and says, "and put up a bolt and doors" (Job 38:8, 10).
orig: ši-ga-ru na-aḫ-ba-l[um? (šigaru naḫbalum), 'bolt, barrier'

p: The lahmu were long-haired beings who served Enki in the waters. An older reading had 'his plants'.
b: Laḫmu means 'hairy'. It names mythical long-haired beings of Enki's waters, his guards and messengers (8:32). SEAL follows F. A. M. Wiggermann (1992) in reading làḫ-mi-šu, 'his hairy ones', here and in the parallel lines; W. G. Lambert and A. R. Millard (1969) read šam-mi-šu, 'his plants'. The newer reading fits the later lines, where the hairy ones carry messages across the sea.
orig: qá-(du làḫ-mi-šu) (qadu laḫmišu), 'with his hairy ones'

p: Lines 7:80–103 are found only in the Assyrian copy, which tells the famine twice.
b: SEAL notes that the Neo-Assyrian copy S+T (column v, lines 3–26) has these lines, while the Middle Babylonian copies X and Y and the Late Babylonian be do not. They run through the same famine that is told more fully in 8:69–99: rain held back above, the deep blocked below, salt in the fields, the old grain eaten, mothers and daughters in the street. The same copy repeats the scene almost word for word later (8:86–99), so the broken words here can be read from there.

p: Salt rising in the soil was a real danger for farmers in southern Mesopotamia.
b: Idrānu is the white salt crust on fields (SEAL, citing Streck 2008). In southern Iraq, irrigation water left salt behind as it dried, and over time fields could turn white and barren. The poem makes this a weapon of the gods. The Bible uses salt land as a picture of judgment: God turns "orchard country into salt land, / because the people living there are evil" (Psalm 107:34; compare Deuteronomy 29:23).
orig: id-[ra-na (idrāna), 'salt'

p: The crop named here is a pulse, perhaps chickpeas.
b: Šû is a field crop. The Akkadian dictionaries disagree: one calls it a kind of grain, the other 'pulse, chick-pea(?)' (SEAL, on the same word at 6:29). The Plain says 'beans', a plain word for a pulse. In the drought no crop comes up, grain or beans.
orig: šu-⌈ú⌉ (šû), 'a pulse'

a: The mother would eat while the daughter watched.
p: This line and the next are told again, more fully, in 8:89–90.
b: These lines belong to the Assyrian expansion (see 7:80) and are repeated in the same copy at 8:89–90, which keeps more of them. The mother eats what food there is and will not share it, and her daughter can only watch. The scene goes on to its terrible end at 8:94–95. The Bible's own famine stories reach the same point (see 8:94).

p: Only 'open her door' survives here. The rest comes from the fuller copy of the same line.
b: The Assyrian copy has only the end of this line. The same copy gives it whole at 8:90: 'the mother would not open her door to her daughter', and SEAL lists the two lines as parallels. The Plain gives the whole line from there.
orig: i-p]a-te bāb(KÁ)-ša (ipatte bābša), 'she opens her door'

p: The first half of this line is restored from 8:93–94.
b: Only the last words, 'for supper, the daughter', survive here. SEAL restores the first half from the matching lines later in the same copy (8:93–94), where the sixth year of famine is named. In the Assyrian copy the lines are packed two to a line, so this one tablet line holds what other copies spread over two.
orig: a-na nap-ta-ni mārta(DUMU.MUNUS) (ana naptani mārta), 'for a meal, the daughter'

p: The rare word šuparkû means a stopping or ending: life about to stop.
b: The line says the people were living 'in the stopping of life', with šuparkû, 'ceasing'. The Plain says their life 'barely held on'. The line returns at 8:99, closing the report of the six years of hunger.
orig: šu-par-k]e-e napištu(ZI) bal-ṭa-at (šuparkê napištu balṭat), 'in the stopping, life lives'

p: Are Atrahasis and Noah the same man? A Christian who believes the Flood happened weighs it.
b: Both are told of a coming flood by heaven, build a boat, save life and offer a sacrifice after. Both are men, not gods. Alan Millard, a Christian Assyriologist, judged that 'the two accounts undoubtedly describe the same Flood', which the Babylonians could only tell 'in their own polytheistic language' while the Hebrews 'understood the action of God in it'. On that view the survivor remembered in Babylon is Noah, renamed and refashioned. Critical scholars treat both as figures of story. Verdict here: likely the same man, if the Flood is history; the stories of his life differ.

a: his god Enki spoke with him
t: A god who speaks to his servant
p: Each Babylonian had a personal god. Enki is Atrahasis' god, and they talk freely.
b: 'His god' (ilšu) is the personal god a Babylonian looked to for protection. SEAL notes that Enki and Atrahasis 'appear to know each other well and speak to each other freely' (on 8:41). The Bible also tells of God speaking with a man before the Flood: "God said to Noah" (Genesis 6:13). But Noah's God is not one god among many. And Jesus calls his own not slaves but friends, "because all I heard from my Father I have let you know" (John 15:15).
orig: il(DINGIR)-šu {d}⌈é-a⌉ it-ti-šú{(erasure?)} i-ta-mu, 'his god Ea spoke with him'

a: He set out on foot from the city.
p: The start of the line is broken. Most scholars restore 'out of the city'.
b: Only '... city, his foot he set' survives. SEAL restores [ina], here 'out of', as W. G. Lambert and A. R. Millard did, because Atrahasis goes to the river (8:14, 8:28). SEAL rejects W. von Soden's restoration, which had Atrahasis stepping 'up' somewhere. The Plain follows the common restoration.
orig: a?⌉-li še-ep-šu iš-ku-un (āli šēpšu iškun), 'city, his foot he set'

a: Day after day he kept weeping.
p: Atrahasis weeps and brings incense day after day. The Bible knows such prayer, and its answer.
b: The verb is again a repeated form: he 'wept and wept'. Prayer with tears is old and human. Hannah wept at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:10), Hezekiah wept bitterly (2 Kings 20:3), and the psalmist said, "A heart broken and crushed, O God, / you will not look down on" (Psalm 51:17). Atrahasis is not sure his god will even hear (8:45). The Psalms are sure that God hears.
orig: ib-ta-na-ak-ki (ibtanakki), 'he kept weeping'

p: Incense went up with prayer in Babylon and in Israel.
b: Muššakku is an incense offering burned for a god. The Bible pairs incense with prayer too: "Let my prayer be set up as incense in front of you" (Psalm 141:2), and in Revelation "the smoke of the incense went up before God, along with the prayers of the saints" (Revelation 8:4). The later copies send Atrahasis to the river at this point (see the variant).
orig: [m]u-uš-ša-ak-ki (muššakki), 'incense'

a: He pleaded on oath with the sage of the gods,
p: The broken start of 8:9–12 is read in several ways. Was Atrahasis pleading, or was the god under oath?
b: SEAL restores [ap]kal, 'the sage of the gods', with W. von Soden, because Enki is named in the matching line (8:11), but notes problems and suggests 'name' instead. William Moran (1987) read the lines as Atrahasis' own words: his god speaks to him but, being under oath, must tell him things in dreams. SEAL thinks that unlikely, since Atrahasis does not speak in the first person here. The Plain gives SEAL's reading: Atrahasis presses his god by oath to answer him in a dream.
orig: ap?]-kal? i-li ta-mi-ma (apkal ilī tamīma), 'sage of the gods, he swore'

p: Atrahasis offers gifts and sleeps by the water hoping for a dream. Solomon received one after sacrifice.
b: Mesopotamians sought messages from their gods in dreams, sometimes by sleeping near a holy place after an offering. Atrahasis does this at the river (8:18–26). The Bible tells of God speaking in dreams: Jacob at Bethel (Genesis 28:12–16), and Solomon after his sacrifices: "It was at Gibeon, in a dream in the night, that the LORD showed himself to Solomon" (1 Kings 3:5). But in the Bible the dream is God's free gift, not something a person can make a god give.
orig: i-na šu-na-a-ti (ina šunāti), 'in dreams'

p: Atrahasis weeps by the river until messengers come. Daniel mourned by the Tigris until a messenger came.
b: By the river, weeping, a man waits for an answer, and messengers from the god cross the water to him (8:37–39). The Bible has a close scene. Daniel mourned three weeks and then stood "beside the great river, the Tigris" (Daniel 10:4), and a heavenly messenger told him: "your words were heard, and it is because of them that I have come" (Daniel 10:12). Exiles also sat "Beside the rivers of Babylon" and wept (Psalm 137:1), and Jews met for prayer by a river at Philippi (Acts 16:13).

p: The Akkadian says 'he divided the night': midnight.
b: Mūšu izūzma means 'he divided the night', an idiom for midnight (George; Streck, cited by SEAL). Atrahasis waits until the river is still and the night is half gone, then makes his offering. Night prayer appears in the Bible too: "Around midnight, as they prayed, Paul and Silas sang God's praises" in prison (Acts 16:25).
orig: mu-šu i-zu-uz-ma (mūšu izūzma), 'the night divided'

p: The word tūʾamtu means 'twin'. Its sense with sleep is not certain.
b: The line pairs šittu, 'sleep', with tūʾamtu, 'twin'. SEAL takes it as a second sleep, after midnight and after the offering, and notes that 'sleep came' is a known way of speaking (Wasserman). Others have understood a sleep that comes in two parts. Either way, Atrahasis falls asleep by the water, hoping for a dream (8:26).
orig: t]u!?-a-am-⸢tum⸣!? (tūʾamtum), 'twin'

p: Atrahasis sends his offering down the river to Enki, who lives in the waters below.
b: Enki's home is the Apsu, the fresh water under the earth, which fed rivers and springs. So the river can carry an offering, and a prayer, down to him, and it does: his weeping 'went down to the Apsu' (8:30). The messengers later confirm that this is how Enki heard (8:51–53). The poem pictures the gods as far off and in need of couriers.

p: Atrahasis asks Enki to remember him. Genesis says God remembered Noah.
b: Ḫasāsu means to call to mind or think of someone. Enki does: 'Enki saw it and remembered you' (8:53). Genesis uses the same idea at the turning point of the Flood: "Then God remembered Noah" (Genesis 8:1). In the Bible, God's remembering is not jogged by a gift floating downstream; it flows from his covenant (Genesis 9:15; Exodus 2:24).
orig: li-iḫ-[su-sa-an-n]i? (liḫsusanni), 'let him remember me'

p: Enki sends his hairy ones across the sea to a weeping man. Are they like the Bible's angels?
b: The Bible's angels are God's messengers too, "spirits in holy service, sent on duty" (Hebrews 1:14), and one came to Daniel by the river (Daniel 10:12). The pattern is shared: a man prays, a god hears, messengers come. But the lahmu are not the same beings. They are servants of one god against the others, they do not know whom they are visiting (8:41), and Atrahasis bows to the ground before them (8:55). Verdict: unlikely to be the same beings; a shared picture of heaven sending word to earth.

p: A place in the god's world and in his temple at Eridu.
b: SEAL explains that the 'quay of the Apsu' is a place in the cosmos and also part of Ea's temple at Eridu, often named in Sumerian spells (citing George 2016). The messengers come from the god's realm across 'the wide sea' (8:37) to the edge of the human world. Temples in Mesopotamia were built to stand for the gods' homes in the cosmos, so a place could be both at once.
orig: ina kar apsî(ABZU) (ina kār apsî), 'at the quay of the Apsu'

p: The messengers do not know Atrahasis; Enki does.
b: Ayyû is 'which' or 'who'. SEAL argues that the words do not mean Enki does not know Atrahasis, since the two speak freely (8:4). It is the messengers who have never met him. They speak to the man as Enki's voice has sent them: 'whoever you are'.
orig: a]-⸢a-ú⸣ ša ta-ba-ak-ku-ú (ayyû ša tabakkû), 'who is it that weeps'

a: Through whom did Enki hear me?
p: Atrahasis is not sure how his prayer got through. The Bible is sure God hears directly.
b: SEAL notes that Atrahasis asks how the message reached Enki even though the poem has just said (8:21): he was not sure the river had carried it. A Babylonian god had to be reached by the right channel. Jesus teaches the opposite: "Your Father knows the things you have need of before you ever ask him" (Matthew 6:8). And when we do not know how to pray, "the Spirit himself pleads for us" (Romans 8:26).

p: The old copy has 'water ... in the night'; the late copies heard it as 'what ... in the night'.
b: The Old Babylonian copy I has mê ina mūši, 'water in the night'. The Middle and Late Babylonian copies X and be have mīnam, 'what?', which SEAL calls a hearing mistake: the words sound alike. The Plain follows the old copy, read as a question.
orig: me-e i-na mu-ši ú-ša-bi-il na-ra (mê ina mūši ušābil nāra), 'water in the night, I made the river carry'

p: Two words for running water are used side by side.
b: Miṭirtu is a canal or stream, nāru a river or watercourse. The poem pairs them, as Hebrew poetry pairs words: 'the canal took it; the river carried it' (8:51). On 'you spoke', which the copy writes as 'he spoke', see the variant.
orig: mi-iṭ-ra-ti na-ri (miṭrati nāri), 'the canal, the river'

p: Atrahasis bows and kisses the ground before the god's messengers. John was told not to.
b: Kissing the ground was how one greeted a king or a god's envoy in the ancient Near East. Atrahasis treats the hairy ones as the god's own presence. When John fell down before the angel who showed him the visions, the angel stopped him: "Do not do it! I am a fellow slave with you ... Worship God!" (Revelation 22:9). The Bible keeps worship for God alone.
orig: iš-šiq qaq-qa-ru (iššiq qaqqaru), 'he kissed the ground'

p: Each great god had a minister who carried his words. Enki's is Usmu; Enlil's is Nusku.
b: A sukkallu was a high official who spoke for his lord. Enlil's minister in Atrahasis is Nusku (9:23); Enki's is Usmu, named here in the Late Babylonian copy be (the old copy is broken). Usmu goes out to Atrahasis with Enki's words (8:61). The chain of messengers shows how distant the gods are imagined to be.
orig: {d}usmû(ARA) ⌈sukkalli(SUKKAL)-šu⌉ (Usmû sukkallišu), 'Usmu, his minister'

a: 'As the people are, so is the state of the land.'
p: Ṭēmu here means the 'state' or 'news' of the land. It is the same word as the slain god's 'understanding'.
b: The line says: 'the ṭēmu of the land is like the ṭēmu of its people'. Ṭēmu covers report, plan, mind and understanding. In Tablet I it is the 'understanding' of the god whose flesh made humans (3:48). Here it means the condition of the land: the land suffers as its people suffer. Hosea has a saying with the same shape: "Like people, like priest" (Hosea 4:9).
orig: ṭè-em māti(KUR) ki-i pī(KA?) ṭè-ma nišī(UN{meš}) (ṭēm māti kī pī ṭēma nišī), 'the state of the land as the state of the people'

t: The land as a fallen man
p: The land is pictured as a young man thrown down on his face.
b: The broken lines 8:63–68 are hard to read; SEAL marks much as uncertain. The image is clear: the land, 'like a young man', has been thrown face down and laid flat. The Bible pictures a ruined land or city as a person too, as when Jerusalem sits "like a widow" (Lamentations 1:1).
orig: bu-up-pa-ni-šá (buppānīša), 'face down'

p: The sky's 'udder' is sealed. The Bible's droughts are warnings meant to turn people back.
b: SEAL takes this line as the start of a report to Enki of what Atrahasis said (the late copy marks a break here, and D has a word showing reported speech). The sky is an udder that gives rain like milk, and Enlil has sealed it. The Bible also tells of a sky shut: "I will make your sky like iron and your ground like bronze" (Leviticus 26:19). But there the drought is a call home: "I myself held back the rain from you / three months before the harvest" (Amos 4:7), and each verse ends, "yet you did not turn back to me" (Amos 4:8).
orig: ka-an-kát? ṣer-ret šá-ma-(a-mi) (kankat ṣerret šamāmi), 'sealed is the udder of the sky'

p: Below, the high water stays in its springs. Genesis has the same springs burst open in the Flood.
b: Naqbu is water rising from under the ground, and mīlu the yearly high water. The river flood that watered the fields does not come. In Genesis the same hidden waters break out in judgment: "all the springs of the great deep burst open" (Genesis 7:11). Here the gods withhold them; in the Flood they will let them loose (9:152).
orig: mi-lu i-na na-aq-b[i] (mīlu ina naqbi), 'the high water in the underground springs'

a: The earth's womb did not give birth.
p: The earth is a mother whose womb gives plants. In drought it bears nothing.
b: The same picture is in the old copies at 6:27 and 6:39, where 'the earth turned its womb' upside down. Genesis also has the earth bring things out at God's word: "Let the land bring out living creatures" (Genesis 1:24). In Genesis the earth is not a goddess; it obeys its maker.
orig: er-ṣe-tum re-e[m-ša] (erṣetum rēmša), 'the earth, its womb'

p: Good farmland was dark; salty land was white.
b: Ṣalmūtum, 'the black ones', are the dark, rich fields; they 'turned white' with salt. The line is the same as 6:38 in the old copies; see the note on salt at 7:84. Ugāru is the common farmland of a town, worked by its people.
orig: ṣa-al-mu-tum ip-ṣú-ú (ṣalmūtum ipṣû), 'the black ones turned white'

a: The first year they ate the old grain.
p: Year by year the hunger gets worse. The Bible's famines are counted in years too.
b: The poem counts six years: first the old grain, then the storehouse, then faces changed, then bodies shrunk, then mothers and daughters sold, then children eaten (8:77–95). The Bible counts famines too: three years in David's time (2 Samuel 21:1), seven in Egypt, where Joseph stored grain ahead: "This food will be a reserve for the land for the seven years of famine" (Genesis 41:36). Joseph's story is one of rescue planned by God (Genesis 50:20).

p: Malt is sprouted barley for beer. The picture is of faces hidden and dull with hunger.
b: Buqlu is malt, barley sprouted and dried for brewing. SEAL explains the covered face as a sign of misery and weakness, and discusses whether malt was kept covered with earth (Stol held so; Sallaberger says tests rule it out). The Assyrian copy says 'dead malt' (variant). Either way, hungry faces look grey and lifeless, like spoiled grain.
orig: ki-ma bu-uq-li (kīma buqli), 'like malt'

p: The verb pictures a field broken up by a harrow, over and over.
b: Šitkuku comes from a verb for harrowing, dragging a tool across a field to break the soil. SEAL takes it as a picture of a life broken down by suffering, as in an Old Babylonian lament that calls a sufferer 'harrowed, broken'. It rejects earlier renderings such as 'little by little' (Foster) or 'tightened' (the Chicago dictionary).
orig: i-na ši-it-ku-ki (ina šitkuki), 'by harrowing'

a: They went bent over in the street.
p: Starving people walk stooped in the street. The prophets saw the same.
b: Qaddiš means 'bent, stooped'. The tall grow short (8:83), the broad grow narrow (8:85). Lamentations describes the same sight in besieged Jerusalem: children "fainting with hunger at every street corner" (Lamentations 2:19), and nobles once "cleaner than snow" now so changed that "no one knows them in the streets" (Lamentations 4:7–8).
orig: ⌈qá⌉-ad-di-iš i-il-la-ka (qaddiš illaka), 'bent, they walk'

a: the scales that weighed out her mother's price
p: Families sold their own members for silver to buy grain. Nehemiah heard the same complaint.
b: SEAL explains the scales: mother and daughter are sold into slavery for silver, weighed out on a balance. In famine, families in the ancient Near East sold or pledged their own people. The Jews of Nehemiah's day said: "we are handing over our sons and daughters to be slaves" (Nehemiah 5:5). In Revelation a rider on a black horse holds "a balance scale in his hand" (Revelation 6:5), a sign of famine prices.
orig: zi-ba-ni-it umme(AMA) (zibānīt ummi), 'the scales of the mother'

a: they set out the daughter for supper
p: The worst year of the famine ends in parents eating children. The Bible tells of this too, and why.
b: SEAL notes that the famine 'aggravates further' until cannibalism comes, and that Assyrian royal annals tell of the same in sieges. The Bible names it as the last curse of a broken covenant: "You will eat the flesh of your sons, and the flesh of your daughters you will eat" (Leviticus 26:29), and records it in Samaria (2 Kings 6:28–29) and Jerusalem: "Women known for compassion boiled their own children with their own hands" (Lamentations 4:10). The difference is the reason. In the poem the gods cause it to get some quiet. In the Bible it is the end of a long road of rebellion, warned of beforehand, lamented by the prophet before God (Lamentations 2:20).
orig: ana nap-⌈ta⌉-ni mārtu(DUMU.MUNUS) (ana naptani mārtu), 'for a meal, the daughter'
r: Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53–57; 2 Kings 6:28–29; Lamentations 2:20; Lamentations 4:10; Jeremiah 19:9

p: The verb is broken, and its meaning is not certain; SEAL takes it as 'consumed'.
b: The Assyrian copy says 'house, one, the other ...' and the verb is broken. SEAL restores and translates it 'consumed'. The sense is that families turned on one another. The same words stood in the shorter repeat at 7:101.
orig: bētu(É) il-ta-nu šanú(2-ú) (bētu iltānu šanû), 'house, one, another'

a: The people's life barely held on."
p: Here the report of the famine ends; only one Old Babylonian copy goes on to tell of Enki's tears.
b: SEAL notes that the Old Babylonian copy I goes straight from the end of Atrahasis' long speech (8:87) to a reaction of Enki (8:100–105), while the copies D, H and S+T skip those lines and jump to another speech of Atrahasis reported to Enki (8:107). So 8:88–99 come from the Assyrian copy alone, and 8:100–105 from I alone.

a: The god heard, and he wept;
p: Enki hears of the famine and weeps. The God of the Bible grieves too, but he is also the Judge.
b: This is the most tender moment in the poem. Enki weeps with pity. The Bible also shows God grieving over humankind: "it pained him to his heart" (Genesis 6:6), and over Israel: "My heart turns over inside me" (Hosea 11:8). Jesus wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). But Enki is one god outvoted by others, and helps by tricks. In the Bible the one who grieves is the same one who judges and the one who saves, so his tears are not helpless.
orig: iš-me-e-ma i-lu i-ba-ak-[ki] (išmēma ilu ibakki), 'the god heard and wept'

p: The word for pity comes from rēmu, which also means 'womb'.
b: Rēmēniš, 'mercifully, in pity', is formed from rēmu, which means both 'womb' and 'compassion' (7:63; 8:72). Hebrew has the same pair: rechem, 'womb', and rachamim, 'compassion', the love of a mother for the child of her body. The Bible uses it of God: "Can a woman forget her nursing baby / and have no pity for the child of her womb?" (Isaiah 49:15).
orig: re-me-ni-iš (rēmēniš), 'mercifully'

a: (An unknown number of lines is lost.)
p: SEAL says the lost lines held Enki's answer, sent through his messengers, and Atrahasis' reply.
b: Copy I breaks off here. SEAL says the missing lines 'contained a speech of Enki/Ea, transmitted by his long-haired heroes to Atra-ḫasīs, and Atra-ḫasīs' answer'. When the text resumes in D, H and the Assyrian copy, the messengers are bringing Atrahasis' answer back to Enki (8:107–118).

p: Niššiku, 'prince', is a title of Enki.
b: The Old Babylonian copy H calls him 'Enki the prince' (niššiku), a title used for him in Tablet I as well, when the gods gave 'the bolt, the barrier of the sea' to 'Enki the prince' (1:15–16). It marks his rank among the great gods.
orig: a-na {d}en-ki ni-iš-ši-ki (ana Enki niššiki), 'to Enki the prince'

p: Atrahasis complains that his god has left him. The Psalms know that cry, and Jesus prayed it.
b: Ezēbu, 'to leave', is the word used in laments. Atrahasis tells Enki: the god of the land has turned on it, and you have left me. The Bible's laments say the same to God: "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?" (Psalm 22:1), the words Jesus cried on the cross (Matthew 27:46). The psalm ends in praise for a God who heard (Psalm 22:24).
orig: te⌉-te-ez-ba-an-ni (tetezbanni), 'you have left me'

a: Let me go down to the Apsu
p: Atrahasis asks to go down to the Apsu and live in Enki's presence.
b: The line uses two place forms (SEAL): 'to the Apsu' and 'in your presence'. Worn out by the famine, Atrahasis asks to leave the human world and live where his god lives. Genesis says of Enoch, before the Flood, "Enoch walked with God. Then he was gone, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24), and Paul wrote, "I long to leave and be with Christ" (Philippians 1:23).
orig: lu-ri-id a[p-sú]m lu-ši-ib (lūrid apsûm lūšib), 'let me go down to the Apsu, let me live'

a: One year they ate the old grain.
p: The Assyrian copy ends with the first line of its next tablet, so a reader knew what came next.
b: This line repeats 8:77. Scribes wrote the first line of the next tablet at the end of each tablet, a 'catchline', so that a set of tablets could be kept in order. Here it shows that the Assyrian edition went on with the famine years, told again, on its next tablet.

a: When the gods were like men
p: The Assyrian copy names the poem 'When the gods were like men' and calls this its first tablet.
b: Babylonian poems were named by their first words. The Old Babylonian title is inūma ilū awīlum, 'When the gods were man' (see 1:1 for that hard line, and the colophon at 9:172). The Assyrian copy writes enūma ilū kī amēli, with kī, 'like': 'When the gods were like men'. It also calls this tablet 'Tablet 1', though it ends deep in the old Tablet II, so the Assyrian edition divided the poem differently.
orig: e-n[u-ma i]lū(d]ingir{meš}) ki-i a-mé-li (enūma ilū kī amēli), 'when the gods like men'

p: This copy belonged to Ashurbanipal, king of Assyria in the 600s BC, who collected Babylonian writings.
b: The colophon reads 'Palace of Ashurbanipal' (Aššur-bāni-apli). Ashurbanipal, the last great king of Assyria, gathered tablets of every kind at Nineveh, and this copy of Atrahasis was among them. The Bible's Assyria of the 700s and 600s BC (2 Kings 17–19) is the world in which this tablet was copied, a thousand years after Ipiq-Aya's.
orig: {m}a[n.šá]r-dù-a (Aššur-bāni-apli), 'Ashurbanipal'

p: A column of one Old Babylonian copy is placed here, but its place is not certain.
b: After 8:118 there is a gap of unknown length. SEAL places column v of the Old Babylonian copy I here as segment F, and estimates that, if so, only five or six lines are missing before and after it. But it warns that it is not certain that I and D had exactly the same text. Atrahasis gathers the elders again (8:134), perhaps to repeat Enki's advice against the famine, as in 7:25–26.

p: Atrahasis calls the elders again, as he did against the plague and the drought.
b: The line matches 5:49 and 7:26. Alan Millard, writing in 1967, could say only that the famine 'may have been stopped by Enki and Atrahasis'. The newer pieces in chapter 9 show how it ended: Enki let the fish of the sea loose (9:18–20, 9:51–54), and Enlil was furious.
orig: ši-bu-ti ú-pa-aḫ-[ḫi-ir (šībūti upaḫḫir), 'he gathered the elders'

p: This chapter joins the Old Babylonian copies D, H, I and C0 with the Middle Babylonian copy X.
b: Segment G follows a short gap. Its lines come from five copies: D (Istanbul), H, I (British Museum), C0 (the Schøyen tablet published by Andrew George in 2009) and the Middle Babylonian X from Babylon, which alone keeps the messengers' trips between Enlil and Enki (9:38–75). SEAL numbers the X-only lines with letters (G 35a–g, G 48a, G 49a–u).

p: The word armannu may be 'apricot'. Its sense here is unclear.
b: Armannu is glossed 'apricot (tree)?' and the verb is 'to smell'. SEAL cites W. von Soden, who understood 'apricot perfume they smelled' again and again. The lines before are broken, so it is not known who smells what. Perhaps the scent of food and plenty reaches Enlil and stirs his anger (9:13).
orig: ar-ma-na i-te-⸢ṣi⸣-i[n (armana iteṣin), 'apricot, he smelled'

p: Enlil is angry because people have food. The God of the Bible is angry at evil, and gives food.
b: SEAL follows von Soden in taking Enlil as the speaker of the next lines. His rage is at the end of the famine: someone has fed the people. Genesis gives the LORD's anger a moral cause: "every plan their hearts shaped was nothing but evil all day long" (Genesis 6:5). And the Psalms praise the God who feeds: "You open your hand / and fill every living thing with what it longs for" (Psalm 145:16).
orig: li-ib-⸢ba⸣-ti ma-l[i (libbāti mali), 'full of rage'

p: Enlil reminds the gods that they all swore together to keep the people starving.
b: Literally 'we brought our mouth together to an oath'. This is the oath of 7:12, by which the great gods agreed to Enlil's plan and each took charge of a part of the world. Enlil treats Enki's release of the fish as breaking it. The line returns at 9:29 and 9:105.
orig: ub-la pí-i-ni iš-ti-[ni-iš (ubla pīni ištiniš), 'we brought our mouth together'

p: Enki 'declared release', a word for setting people free. The Bible proclaims release as God's own work.
b: My own comparison, not the poem's meaning. Andurāru is 'freedom, release', and ulla a collar or yoke. Enlil uses them as charges: Enki undid the yoke and freed the people from hunger. The Bible's year of Jubilee commands the same kind of act: "proclaim release in the land for all who live in it" (Leviticus 25:10), and Jesus read in Nazareth that he was sent "to proclaim release to the captives" (Luke 4:18). In Atrahasis release is a crime against the high god. In the Bible it is what God himself proclaims.
orig: ul-l[a (ulla), 'yoke'

p: Enki sets free the fish of the sea to feed the starving. The Bible's God feeds crowds with bread and fish.
b: Mišertu is the produce of sea and rivers: fish. SEAL notes the play of sound in the line (umaššer ... mišerta). The famine ends with a flood of fish (9:51–54). Moses once asked, "If all the fish of the sea were gathered for them, would there be enough for them?" (Numbers 11:22). Jesus fed thousands with loaves and fish (Matthew 14:19; John 6:11) and filled his disciples' net (John 21:6). In the Bible the giver of food is not breaking the rules of heaven; he is heaven's King.
orig: ni-ši mi-še-er-ta (nišī mišerta), 'for the people, the sea's produce'

a: a sign in the ... of the sun
p: The word left blank, ašqulālu, is not understood.
b: The line says Enki 'set a sign' (itta šakānu) 'in the ašqulālu of the sun'. The meaning of ašqulālu is unknown; SEAL gives studies of the word and notes that B. R. Foster restored '[shade?]'. Some sign in the sky marked what Enki had done, but no one can yet say what. The Plain leaves the word as a gap rather than guess.
orig: aš-qú-la-⸢lu⸣ ša-am-ši (ašqulālu šamši), 'the ašqulālu of the sun'

p: Enlil sends for two companions, probably the gods Shullat and Hanish.
b: SEAL accepts von Soden's reading itbāru, 'companion', which replaces older readings of the line. Von Soden took the two as the gods Shullat and Hanish, who appear together later, going before the flood (9:147). They act here as Enlil's messengers to Enki.
orig: ⸢še-na⸣ i[t-b]a-⸢ri⸣ (šena itbāri), 'two companions'

p: A shar is 3,600; 'shar upon shar' means a vast swarm.
b: The line counts the fish in šār, 3,600, the largest round number of Babylonian counting: 'fish to a shar of fish, one shar each'. SEAL renders it as one myriad after another. When the bolt broke, the sea poured out fish beyond counting.
orig: ana šār(ŠÁR) nūnī(KU6{meš}) 1 šār(ŠÁR){ta.àm} (ana šār nūnī 1 šār.TA.ÀM), 'to a shar of fish, a shar each'

p: Enki says the sea's guards broke the bolt and he could not stop them. The Bible's sea obeys God.
b: Enki's defense is that the bolt of the sea, his charge (7:74), was broken by others. Gods in this poem can lose control of their part of the world. The Bible's God never does: "Up to here you may come, but not one step more" (Job 38:11). When Jesus spoke to the sea, "Quiet! Be muzzled!", the disciples asked, "Who can this be? The wind and the sea both do what he says!" (Mark 4:39, 41).
orig: iš-bi-ru mi-šil-šu (išbirū mišilšu), 'they broke half of it'

a: I struck down the guards of the sea.
p: SEAL thinks this Middle Babylonian line arose from a misunderstanding of the old text at 9:122.
b: The Old Babylonian form of Enki's answer names the two 'gatekeepers' who broke the bolt: atûma malukkû tiāmtum (9:122). SEAL argues that the scribe of X did not know the rare malukku, wrote the common maṣṣaru, 'guard', and that his addukū, 'I killed', may be a mishearing of atûma, 'gatekeepers'. If so, the killing of the guards is a scribe's invention.
orig: ad⸣-du-⌈ku⌉ ma-aṣ-ṣa-ru tam-ti (addukū maṣṣarū tâmti), 'I killed the guards of the sea'

a: I laid a penalty on them a second time."
p: Enki blames the sea's gatekeepers and says he punished them. It recalls Adam blaming Eve.
b: My own comparison. Charged with freeing the fish, Enki says he did his duty, that others broke the bolt, and that he punished them, twice. He never says he was sorry for the people, though he had wept for them (8:102). Genesis has the first human answer the same way: "The woman! You set her at my side, and she is the one who gave me some from the tree, so I ate" (Genesis 3:12). The poem's gods behave like people caught out; the Bible's God is the one who asks the questions.

a: Come, all of us, to the oath of the flood!
t: An oath to destroy, an oath to spare
p: The gods swear to bring the flood. In the Bible God swears never to send it again.
b: Enlil makes the whole assembly swear to the flood: Anu first, then Enlil and his sons (9:79–80). The Bible turns this upside down. God swears an oath after the Flood: "as I swore that Noah's waters / would never again sweep over the earth" (Isaiah 54:9), and makes a covenant: "there will not again be a flood to ruin the earth" (Genesis 9:11). Hebrews says God "swore an oath by himself" to make his promise sure (Hebrews 6:13). The poem's oath binds the gods to destroy; God's oath binds himself to mercy.
orig: a-na ma-mi-⌈tam⌉ a-bu-bi (ana māmītam abūbi), 'to the oath of the flood'

p: Abūbu is the Akkadian word for the Flood. Genesis has its own word, mabbul.
b: Abūbu is 'the flood, the deluge'. The site writes it in lowercase, 'the flood', as its Genesis does: "I am going to bring the flood" (Genesis 6:17). The Hebrew word there, mabbul, is used only of Noah's Flood: in Genesis 6–11 and once in the Psalms, "At the Flood the LORD took his throne" (Psalm 29:10). Both languages have a special word for that one event.
orig: a-bu-bi (abūbi), 'the flood'

p: The gods swear by rank: Anu, then Enlil and his sons. Enki will refuse.
b: The order follows the gods' rank: Anu, the father in the sky; Enlil, lord of the earth; then Enlil's sons. Only the Middle Babylonian copy X keeps 9:77–80. Enki is not named among those who swore here. In 9:136–141 the gods try to bind him too, and he refuses. In Tablet III he keeps the oath's letter by speaking to a reed wall instead of to Atrahasis (chapter 10).
orig: it-ta-mi mārū(DUMU{meš})-šú it-ti-šú ta-mu-ni (ittami mārūšu ittišu tamûni), 'he swore, his sons with him swore'

a: Anu took flight in the heavens.
p: The line comes from C0, a copy published in 2009. SEAL takes it as Anu rising higher in the sky.
b: Lines 9:87–162 come mostly from C0 (MS 5108), published by Andrew George in 2009. The verb is naprušu, 'to fly'. SEAL assumes that Anu leaves his post in the sky and rises to a higher sphere, but the sense is not certain. What follows is plenty: water from the deep covers the plain and the meadows fill (9:88–93). The order of events here is not clear.
orig: an-nu-um (Annum), 'Anu'

a: The meadows filled up with plants
p: Water from the deep brings grass and grain again. The Psalms praise God for the same.
b: The release of the waters ends the famine. Psalm 104 praises God for this order of things: "He sends springs out into the stream valleys" and "He makes green grass sprout for the herds, / and crops for the work of human hands, / so that bread comes up out of the ground" (Psalm 104:10, 14). There is no rival god to break the rules; the Creator keeps the world supplied.

p: The people eat again. Jesus reminded the tempter that bread is not all a person lives by.
b: After six years of hunger the people eat and are fed. Bread is life in the poem. Jesus, hungry in the wilderness, answered: "People will not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes out of God's mouth" (Matthew 4:4). The Bible honors bread as God's gift (Psalm 104:14) and points beyond it to himself: "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35).

p: Ṣīḫtu usually means laughter. Some read it here as vexation or bitter laughter.
b: The line says ṣīḫtum 'ate' Enki in the gods' assembly. Andrew George took it as 'vexation'; W. von Soden kept 'laughter', a bitter one; SEAL follows George. The line before has a related debate: B. R. Foster, after von Soden, has Enki 'fretting at sitting idle', while SEAL takes 'sitting' as the setting, not the cause. Either way Enki sits in the council, angry, and laughs or seethes. The Bible has God laugh at rebels from his throne: "Seated in the heavens, he laughs" (Psalm 2:4).
orig: ṣi-iḫ-tum i-ku-ul-šu (ṣīḫtum īkulšu), 'laughter ate him'

a: What did Anu and Adad guard
p: Enki asks what each god guarded, to show that his own post was the one that failed through others.
b: Mīna is 'what?'. SEAL translates 'Why did Anum (and) Adad guard ...', but the word may be 'what'. Enki turns Enlil's words back on him: each god had a post, and his was given him by them all (9:117).
orig: mi-na (mīna), 'what'

a: my arm was placed there by all of you
p: Enki says the gods put him in charge; the broken verb is read in different ways.
b: The copy reads 'my arm by all of you was pl[aced]'. SEAL takes it as Enki saying that he acted with authority given by all the gods, and restores šaknat. Andrew George read 'my arm was tugged' (šadat), which SEAL finds hard to fit. The point is Enki's defense: I did my part as you assigned it.
orig: a-ḫi!(text: IḪ) i-na ka-li-ku-nu (aḫi ina kalīkunu), 'my arm by all of you'

a: One of them held back shar upon shar of fish;
p: 'One' and 'the second' are the two gatekeepers of the sea named in 9:122.
b: SEAL, following George, explains that 'the first' and 'the second' are the two water beings named in 9:122, whose job was to hold in the fish. One held a shar of fish back; the other started a fight, and between them they broke the great bolt.
orig: iš-ti-nu-um-ma ú-ke-e[l] (ištīnumma ukēl), 'the first held'

p: The gatekeepers are Malukku and Tiamtum, 'the Sea'. Malukku may lie behind a name in Berossus.
b: Atû is 'gatekeeper'. Malukku is a rare word. Andrew George links it to emarukku, a 'flood dragon', and to Omorka, a name in the Babyloniaca of Berossus, the Babylonian priest who wrote a history in Greek about 280 BC (SEAL; W. G. Lambert read the word differently). Tiāmtum is the common noun 'sea'; Alan Millard notes that in Atrahasis it is not the dragon Tiamat of the Enuma Elish. The link to Berossus is possible, not proven.
orig: a-tu-ú-ma ma-lu-[k]u-ú (atûma malukkû), 'the gatekeepers, Malukku'

t: A speech from Tablet I repeated
p: The lines repeat part of Mami's speech after she made humankind. SEAL thinks she speaks here.
b: SEAL notes that 9:128–137 repeat in part the speech of the birth goddess Mami in Tablet I (3:73–79), after she made the first humans: the heavy work, the work basket, the noise, the slain god. SEAL assumes that Mami speaks here too, and that Enki's answer (9:139) is to the whole assembly. She reminds the gods of what they did when they made humankind, and proposes to bind Enki by oath (9:136).

p: The line repeats 3:76, where the noise is something the gods gave humankind.
b: The verb, restored from 3:76, is the hard word of that line, which describes noise given to humankind (ana awīlūti). If the gods themselves gave humans their noise, Enlil's complaint is about something built into the people the gods made. The poem does not stop to ask whose fault the noise is.
orig: ri-ig-m[a (rigma), 'noise'

a: Let it go back into its socket.
p: Uppu is a tube or socket: 'let it go back into its hole' means 'let it be undone'.
b: SEAL follows W. von Soden in restoring uppīša, 'its socket', and in taking the line to mean that something should vanish completely. What is to be undone is broken in the line before (perhaps a decree or plan). The speaker wants the gods to reverse course and bind Enki (9:136).
orig: a-na up-[pí-ša] (ana uppīša), 'to its socket'

p: The gods want to make Enki swear, so he cannot help humankind again.
b: The copy's verb nu-ta-am-MU-NI is taken, with von Soden, as a slip for nutammi, 'let us make swear'. Massû, 'leader, expert', is restored. Enki is the wise one, the expert, and so the danger: he keeps finding ways around Enlil's plans. Binding him by oath would close the last door. He refuses (9:140), but in Tablet III he still keeps to the oath's letter (chapter 10).
orig: n[u-t]a-am-MU-NI ma-ás-s[a!-am] (nutammi massâm), 'let us make the expert swear'

a: Should I bring my hand down on my own people?
p: Enki will not swear to destroy the people he made. Who in the Bible both judges and saves?
b: Enki calls humans 'my people' (nišīya): he planned their making (chapter 3). He refuses to harm them, and leaves the flood to Enlil (9:145). The poem splits the roles: one god destroys, another warns. In Genesis one God does both. He says, "I am going to bring the flood" (Genesis 6:17), and in the same speech, "But with you I will set up my covenant" (Genesis 6:18). Abraham could ask him, "Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?" (Genesis 18:25), because judging and saving belong to one just God, who takes "no pleasure in the death of a wicked man" (Ezekiel 33:11).
orig: ú-ub-ba-al qá-ti a-na n[i-ši-ia(-ma)] (ubbal qāti ana nišīya), 'I bring my hand to my people'

p: The line is broken. Older editions restored 'I do not know'; SEAL reads it as Enki asking who will do it.
b: The line reads 'who is he? I ...'. Since Lambert and Millard (1969), editors have restored 'I do not know' and taken 'he' as the flood. SEAL objects that 'who?' cannot refer to a flood, and takes it to mean the one who will make it. The next lines fit: 'Am I the one to give birth to [the flood]?' (9:144; the restoration is from the Akkadian dictionary of von Soden and from Lambert and Millard) and 'Its work lies with ...' (9:145), which Lambert and Millard took as Enlil's task.
orig: ma-an-nu šu-ú a-na-ku (mannu šū anāku), 'who is he? I'

t: The gods who go before the flood
p: Shullat and Hanish lead the storm here and in the Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI.
b: SEAL lists 9:147–151 as parallel to lines 100–103 of the Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI, where the gods Shullat and Hanish also go before the storm, a god tears out posts, and the throne-bearers march. Alan Millard judged that Tablet XI of Gilgamesh drew its Flood story from Atrahasis: 'a case of literary borrowing cannot be doubted'. Verdict: a direct literary link between the two Babylonian poems.
orig: {d}šu-ul-la-at ù {d}[ḫa-ni-iš] (Šullat u Ḫaniš), 'Shullat and Hanish'

p: The god who 'leads on' is the throne-bearer of the gods. Scholars differ on who he is.
b: C0 keeps guzalû, 'throne-bearer'. Andrew George restores Adad at the end of the line. SEAL notes that in the Epic of Gilgamesh Ninurta is called the throne-bearer and suggests Ninurta here, while in another line of Gilgamesh the same title is given to Shullat and Hanish.
orig: guzalûm({giš}GU.⌈ZA⌉.<LÁ>) (guzalûm), 'throne-bearer'

a: Let the waters spill over; let the outlet grow wide.
p: Enki tells the gods how the flood will come: water from below breaking out.
b: Arūru is the outlet of a canal; SEAL, following George, takes it as the mythic outlet of the water under the earth. The waters held back in the famine (8:71) will now burst out. Genesis tells it the same way: "all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the windows of the sky were opened" (Genesis 7:11).
orig: a-ru-r[u-u]m (arūrum), 'the outlet'

t: A day set for the flood
p: The flood is set for the day of the new moon. Genesis gives the Flood a date too.
b: Ūm warḫim is the day of the new moon, the start of a month. Enki names the day the work will be done. Genesis also dates the Flood to a day: "In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month" (Genesis 7:11).
orig: a-na ú-um wa-⌈ar⌉-ḫ[i-im] (ana ūm warḫim), 'for the day of the month'

p: Adad's 'noise' is thunder. The gods answer human noise with their own.
b: Rigmu is the same word as the noise of humankind (7:16, 7:67). Said of Adad, the storm god, it is thunder. The poem's gods, troubled by human noise, will answer it with the roar of the storm. The Bible gives thunder to the LORD alone: "The LORD's voice is over the waters" (Psalm 29:3), the psalm that ends at the Flood (Psalm 29:10).
orig: ⌈ri⌉-ig-ma-⌈a⌉-a[m (rigmam), 'noise'

p: C0 spells the hero's name with an extra w: Watram-hasis.
b: This copy writes wa-at-ra-am-ḫa-sí-i-sí. Most copies write Atram-hasis or Atra-hasis. The name means 'exceedingly wise' (see the note at its first use in the book). The broken lines that follow (9:159–163) speak of Atrahasis, his work and his stores; they seem to look ahead to Enki's warning in Tablet III.
orig: wa-a[t-ra-am-ḫa-sí-i-sí (Watram-hasis)

p: SEAL reads the sign as 'evil'; earlier editors read it differently.
b: Copy D has 'do not listen to ...' followed by a sign SEAL reads as ḪUL, 'evil', with caution, where Lambert and Millard read other signs. SEAL compares the Epic of Gilgamesh, Tablet XI, where a goddess regrets that she 'spoke evil' in the assembly of the gods. The speaker here is not known; perhaps it is Enki, telling Atrahasis what the gods have done.
orig: e ta-aš-mi-a a-na Ḫ[UL (ē tašmiā ana lemutti), 'do not listen to evil'

p: Gamertu means 'complete destruction'. Genesis' God also speaks of an end of all flesh.
b: The gods 'commanded gamertu', destruction to the end. Genesis uses words just as strong: "I will wipe out the humankind I created from the face of the ground" (Genesis 6:7), and "The end of all flesh is coming before me" (Genesis 6:13). Yet in Genesis the end is not total: "But Noah found favor in the LORD's eyes" (Genesis 6:8).
orig: ga-me-[er-tam] (gamertam), 'total destruction'

a: Enlil has done an evil work against the people."
p: In the poem the evil is the god's. In Genesis the evil is humanity's, and God is just.
b: Tablet II ends with a plain verdict: Enlil's work against the people is evil. The poem does not hide that its high god is unjust. Genesis puts the evil elsewhere: "every plan their hearts shaped was nothing but evil all day long" (Genesis 6:5), and the earth was "full of violence" (Genesis 6:11). The Bible's Judge does what is right (Genesis 18:25), and grieves (Genesis 6:6). Asked who sends the Flood and who warns the survivor, the poem names two gods at odds; Genesis names one God, just and merciful at once.
orig: [ši-i]p-ra l[e-em-n]a a-na ni-ši (šipra lemna ana nišī), 'an evil work against the people'

a: Atrahasis opened his mouth to speak,
p: SEAL notes that these lines are also the opening lines of Tablet III, now broken there.
b: SEAL notes that 9:168–169 serve as the catchline of Tablet III in the Old Babylonian edition from Sippar, whose own first lines are broken. Atrahasis' answer to his lord begins the next tablet (chapter 10), where Enki gives him the dream and the warning.

p: Copy B ends its last column with a line count, the title, the scribe and the date.
b: Copy B's last column notes '37' lines. SEAL works out from this that the first 34 lines of the column are lost. Then comes the colophon, the scribe's signature at the end of the tablet: the title, the total of 439 lines for Tablet II, the scribe's name and the date. The generated text marks this line as lost, but SEAL's score of B shows the number.

p: The Old Babylonian copy names the poem by its first line, inūma ilū awīlum.
b: The title is the first line of the poem, inūma ilū awīlum. On how to translate it, see 1:1. The Assyrian copy gave a smoother form, 'When the gods were like men' (8:120). Titles taken from first lines are also how the Hebrew Bible names its books: Genesis is Bereshit, 'In the beginning'.
orig: i-nu-ma i-lu a-wi-lum (inūma ilū awīlum), 'when the gods man'

p: Ipiq-Aya copied Tablet II in the 11th year of King Ammi-saduqa, about 1628 BC.
b: SEAL reads the scribe's name as Ipiq-Aya (after Wilcke). The same junior scribe signed Tablet I, in the month of Nisan, and Tablet III, in the month of Ayyaru; Tablet II is dated to Shabatu, day 28. SEAL identifies the year name, 'Ammi-saduqa built Dur-Ammi-saduqa at the mouth of the Euphrates', as year 11 of Ammi-saduqa of Babylon, about 1628 BC. Ipiq-Aya worked at Sippar. Ammi-saduqa was the fourth king after Hammurabi.
orig: SIG-{d}a-a dub-sar tur (Ipiq-Aya ṭupšarru ṣeḫru), 'Ipiq-Aya, junior scribe'
